title: What is the point of the "NewTarget is equal to the active function object" in [HTMLConstructor]?

labels.name: topic: custom elements
labels.description: Relates to custom elements (as defined in DOM and HTML)

body:
I am trying to understand the point of https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/dom.html#htmlconstructor step 2, which says:

2. If NewTarget is equal to the active function object, then throw a TypeError.

There is then a note that says:

> If this check was not present, it would be possible to create an instance of HTMLButtonElement whose local name was bad-1.

I believe that claim in the note is, luckily, untrue.  Indeed, assume the check in step 2 is removed.  Now there are two cases:

* In the first case, the definition didn't use "extends", so we enter step 4.  In that case we enforce that the active function is HTMLElement and when we create the element we create an instance of HTMLElement with whatever custom element name the definition that uses NewTarget as ctor was registered for.  This is OK, from a basic sanity point of view.

* In the second case, the definition used "extends", so we enter step 5.  In that case we ensure that _definition_'s local name is a _valid local name_ for the active function object.  That is, we ensure that if the active function object is HTMLButtonElement, then the local name is in fact "button".  We then proceed to create an element with that local name, which is still all sane.

I say "luckily", because of course it's possible to invoke any constructor with any newTarget via `Reflect.construct`.  So it's always possible to get past the check in step 2 if one really wants to.

So what does step 2 really do?  Well, it prevents using an element interface as the constructor in a custom element definition.  But why is this something we really need to prevent?  It seems to me that if step 2 were taken out then all you would be able to do that you can't do now is:

    customElements.define("my-el", HTMLElement);

such that `new HTMLElement` now constructs a `<my-el>` and

    customElements.define("my-el", HTMLQuoteElement, { extends: "q" });

such that `new HTMLQuoteElement` constructs a `<q>`.  So effectively "bind" an element constructor to one and only one of the allowed tag names for that constructor....  Maybe preventing this is worthwhile, but I'd like to see the reasoning for it.  If there isn't a good reason for it, I'd like to remove the complexity.

@domenic @annevk
